newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Tate & Lyle H1 profits to plummet.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Tate & Lyle H1 profits to plummet.

text.p: British sweetener and animal feed producer Tate & Lyle Plc is forecast to report a sharp drop in its half-year profits on Wednesday, mainly hit by a very poor performance from A.E. Staley, its U.S. high fructrose sugar producer.

Analysts forecasts range from 112.7 million to 129 million stg, down significantly from last years figure of 168.2 million. A dividend of between 5.3 and 5.7 pence per share is forecast, against 5.3p last time.

Analysts estimate that Staley's profits will halve to some 30 million stg, squeezed on the one hand by overcapacity in the industry and high corn prices and on the other by its inability to pass that added cost onto the consumer.
High fructose corn syrup is used as a sweetener in soft drinks like Coca Cola and Pepsi and supply contracts to these soft drinks firms are re-negotiated every calendar year.

Larry Pillard, Tate's chief executive, told Reuters in February that fructose contract prices for 1997, which largely had been set, were lower than a year earlier as were corn costs. He blamed lower margins on overcapacity in the U.S. fructrose industry.

Staley's output accounts for a little over 20 percent of total U.S. fructose production. Demand for high fructose corn syrup in the United States is currently running at about 70 percent of the industry's capacity.

In January the company also issued a profits warning, saying it expected results for the six months to March 1997 to be below the year earlier half but above the second half of the 1996 financial year.
The company made pre-tax profits of 168.2 million stg in the six months to March 30, 1996 and full-year profits of 276.3 million, down 11.2 percent on the year.
Tate said the strength of sterling adversely affected profit before tax for the first quarter ended December 1996 by 7.1 million stg.

As well as an adverse currency impact of 10-15 million stg at the half year, analysts also expect profits from the group's Australian unit to fall some 10 million, as competition stiffens in the region.
